aiSummary: In ancient Greek and Roman thought, literary creation was rooted in mimesis (imitation) and imitatio, with theorists like Plato and Aristotle viewing art as an imitation of nature or ideal forms, not novel invention. Roman writers and educators, including Quintilian, encouraged emulation of canonical authors through creative variation and rivalry, valuing imitation as a creative art. Originality in the modern sense was not prominent; Latin literature relied on allusion and adaptation, with authors like Virgil and Ovid praised for eloquence and innovation in traditional material rather than new content. Imitation was seen as a continuous, cumulative process, as noted by Ernst Robert Curtius, where material was transformed into something distinct yet familiar, akin to Seneca’s metaphor of a bee combining nectar. In the Middle Ages, authorship was defined by auctoritas (authority) rather than originality, with scholars fearing novelty as heresy; the Latin word auctor implied a trusted source, and 13th-century scholastics, such as St. Bonaventure, distinguished roles like scribe, compiler, commentator, and author, emphasizing collaboration and tradition. While originality was acknowledged in the auctor’s work, it was viewed as part of a collective enterprise, with all writing types—transcription, compilation, commentary, and authorship—considered valid.

title: Originality in Classical Thought
